title: Skilled immigration
log: 2026-11-01T14:46:37Z match: Claude Haiku 5.5 found no bank point the same, so it is written new
2026-11-02T04:35:39Z autoreview: cleared with the fix (card wording, b wording, b wording)

match.reason: None of the bank points teach skilled immigration as a supply-side policy; the closest, Aggregate supply and productivity, covers the general idea of inputs and productivity but not migration as a policy lever.

draft.title: Skilled immigration
card: Skilled immigration is a policy of letting in migrants who have skills the economy needs, such as nurses, engineers or electricians. It is an aggregate supply policy because it aims to raise the economy's productive capacity.
Migrants add to the population and the labour force. A larger labour force means more workers are available to produce goods and services.
Skilled migrants can fill skill gaps, where employers cannot find enough local workers for a job. Filling these gaps can ease labour shortages and let businesses keep producing.
Migrants are often of working age, so they can lift the participation rate and productivity. Over time, the larger and more skilled workforce can lift potential output.
draft.remember: Skilled immigration grows the workforce and fills skill gaps, which can raise productive capacity.

a.q: A regional Victorian hospital cannot hire enough local radiographers, so it recruits some from overseas. Which supply-side effect does this show?
opts: It fills a skill gap and adds to the labour force
It cuts tariffs so that imported inputs cost less
It puts a price on pollution to change firm costs
It raises the price level by lifting consumer demand
a.why: The hospital could not find local workers for a role, and migrants fill that gap while adding to the labour force. Demand effects may follow, but the policy is about raising productive capacity, so the demand option is wrong.
a.clue: Think about what the hospital lacked.

b.q: Tariq runs a building firm in Geelong. Electricians are scarce, so his projects are delayed. How could a rise in skilled immigration help the wider economy?
opts: More electricians could ease the shortage and lift output
More workers would cut the size of the labour force
Higher migration would lower potential output at once
Migrants would raise costs by adding to total demand only
b.why: More electricians fill the skill gap, so projects can go ahead and output can rise. The demand-only option is tempting because migrants also spend, but the policy also adds to the labour force and productive capacity.
b.clue: Which option adds to what the economy can produce?

a.best: It fills a skill gap and adds to the labour force

b.best: More electricians could ease the shortage and lift output

problems.detail: "Migrants are often of working age, so they can lift the participation rate and productivity" ties productivity to being working age. Productivity gains come from migrants' skills, not their age, so the causal link misleads. Age explains the participation effect only.

The right option is the only one with the hedge "could"; the other three use "would". The distractors are also plainly absurd for Year 12, such as a larger workforce cutting the labour force. A student could pick the answer without knowing the idea.
The distractor "Migrants would raise costs by adding to total demand only" uses "only" and "would", where the card speaks of what immigration "can" do.

check.summary: Question b's right option stands out as the only hedged, sensible choice among absurd distractors. The card also wrongly implies that being working age lifts productivity, when that effect comes from skills.

proposal.title: Skilled immigration
card: Skilled immigration lets in migrants with skills the economy needs, such as nurses, engineers or electricians. It is an aggregate supply policy because it aims to raise the economy's productive capacity.
Migrants add to the population and the labour force. A larger labour force means more workers are available to produce goods and services.
Skilled migrants can fill skill gaps, where employers cannot find enough local workers for a job. Filling these gaps can ease labour shortages and let businesses keep producing.
Migrants are often of working age, which can lift the participation rate. Their skills and training can lift productivity, the output produced per hour worked.
proposal.remember: Skilled immigration can grow the workforce, fill skill gaps and raise what the economy can produce over time.

a.q: A regional Victorian hospital cannot hire enough local radiographers, so it recruits some from overseas. Which supply-side effect does this show?
opts: It fills a skill gap and adds to the labour force
It lifts productivity because the staff are of working age
It adds to demand but leaves productive capacity unchanged
It eases the shortage but shrinks the population
a.why: The hospital could not find local workers for a role, and the migrants fill that gap while adding to the labour force. Being of working age explains a rise in participation, not productivity, which comes from skills.
a.clue: Think about what the hospital lacked.

b.q: Tariq runs a building firm in Geelong. Electricians are scarce, so his projects are delayed. How could a rise in skilled immigration help the wider economy?
opts: More electricians could ease the shortage and lift output
Migrants could lift productivity by being of working age
Migrants could lift spending but not what the economy makes
Electricians could lift participation through their skills
b.why: More electricians fill the skill gap, so delayed projects can go ahead and output can rise. Being of working age can lift participation, but productivity gains come from migrants' skills, so the age option mixes up the two effects.
b.clue: Which effect comes from age, and which from skills?
